title: When classical ML beats a neural network, which is often
story:
The methods that transformed images and language get treated as a general ranking, as though everything else were a weaker version of the same thing. On the data most organisations actually hold — rows and columns, a few thousand to a few hundred thousand of them — that ranking is not what the evidence shows.

Grinsztajn, Oyallon and Varoquaux benchmarked it properly in 2022, across 45 datasets with clear tabular characteristics, comparing standard and novel deep learning methods against tree-based models, with a methodology that accounted for both fitting the models and finding good hyperparameters. That last point is what makes the result worth citing: the usual objection to such comparisons is that the neural network was under-tuned, and the benchmark was constructed to answer it.

Three findings. Tree-based models remain state of the art on medium-sized data, of the order of ten thousand samples, even without accounting for their superior speed. The performance gap is not mostly due to categorical features — the standard explanation, that neural networks merely need better encodings, does not account for it. And the gap does not disappear after tuning hyperparameters, which removes the other standard explanation.

The interesting part is the why, and their analysis points at inductive bias rather than capacity. Tabular columns are heterogeneous and individually meaningful in a way pixels are not: column seven is annual income, and its neighbour is a postcode, and there is no translation invariance or locality to exploit because the ordering of columns carries no information. A method that selects among features suits that structure. A method built to compose and transform a homogeneous input is solving a problem the data does not pose. They identify robustness to uninformative features as a desirable bias for this setting — real tables contain many columns that carry nothing, and a splitting method simply never splits on them, while a dense architecture has to learn to ignore each one.

Two honest qualifications. This is an empirical result in a stated regime — those datasets, that size, that tuning budget — and it is not a theorem about all tabular problems forever. And the authors are careful that their findings do not contradict work claiming benefits from regularisation for tabular data, since adequate regularisation and careful optimisation may let neural networks learn irregular patterns. The defensible claim is not that one family is better. It is that the newer family is not the default here, and that treating it as the default costs accuracy, time and interpretability at once.

problem.name: Matching method to data structure
problem.shape: A method has to be chosen for a problem, and the most prominent family was designed for a kind of data this is not.
tell: the data is rows and columns with individually meaningful fields
the dataset is thousands to hundreds of thousands of rows
many columns carry little or nothing
a neural network was chosen before the data was characterised
problem.move: Characterise the data before choosing the family. For heterogeneous columns at moderate scale, fit a gradient-boosted tree ensemble first and treat it as the number to beat. Reach for a neural network when the data has structure worth exploiting — order, locality, or a modality where representations transfer — and justify it against the tree result rather than instead of it.
problem.invariant: Performance follows the match between a method's inductive bias and the data's structure. Tabular columns are heterogeneous, individually meaningful and often uninformative, and their order carries no information.
problem.breaks: This is an empirical finding within a stated regime — a particular collection of datasets, of the order of ten thousand samples, with a defined tuning budget — not a theorem. The authors note their results do not contradict claims that adequate regularisation and careful optimisation may let neural networks learn irregular patterns.

cost.time: fitting the simpler family first costs a little time and usually returns it, since these models train in minutes rather than hours
cost.space: smaller models, no accelerator requirement, and an inspectable structure
cost.beats: starting with the most prominent method, which on this kind of data tends to cost accuracy, training time and interpretability simultaneously

worked.problem: Why is the newer method not the default choice on tabular data?
worked.reasoning:
Because the properties that make it powerful elsewhere are properties this data does not have, and that was measured rather than assumed.

Take the measurement first, since the claim is otherwise just a preference. The benchmark covered 45 datasets with clear tabular characteristics, compared standard and novel deep learning methods against tree-based models, and accounted for both fitting and hyperparameter search — which matters, because the standing objection to such comparisons is that the network was under-tuned. The findings were that tree-based models remain state of the art on medium-sized data, of the order of ten thousand samples, even before their speed advantage is counted; that the gap is not mostly due to categorical features; and that it does not disappear after tuning. Those two negative findings remove the usual explanations.

Then the reason, which is about inductive bias rather than capacity. In an image, neighbouring pixels are related, the same pattern means the same thing anywhere in the frame, and the input is homogeneous — so architectures built on locality and weight sharing are encoding something true about the data. A table has none of that. Column seven is annual income and column eight is a postcode; their adjacency is an artefact of how the file was written, and permuting the columns changes nothing about the problem. There is no locality to exploit and no translation invariance to assume, so the machinery that makes those architectures effective has nothing to attach to.

Meanwhile the structure a table does have suits splitting. Columns are individually meaningful, so a method that selects among them and thresholds them is working at the natural grain of the data. Real tables carry many columns that contain nothing, and a splitting method simply never splits on them, while a dense architecture must learn to ignore each one — which is why the analysis identifies robustness to uninformative features as a desirable bias here.

I would give two qualifications rather than overclaim. It is an empirical result in a stated regime, and at much larger scale, or where pretrained representations transfer, the picture can differ. And the authors are explicit that their findings do not contradict work claiming benefits from regularisation for tabular data, since adequate regularisation and careful optimisation may allow neural networks to learn irregular patterns.

So the practical answer is not that one family is better. It is that on this kind of data the tree ensemble is the number to beat, it takes minutes to produce, and choosing otherwise without beating it costs accuracy, time and interpretability at once.

problem.practice: Take a tabular problem you have solved with a neural network and fit a gradient-boosted tree ensemble on the same split, with a comparable tuning budget. Record both scores and both training times. Then count how many of your columns carry almost no signal, and check which model was obliged to learn to ignore them.

beats.broke: The methods that transformed perception problems get assumed to be the strongest option everywhere, so they are reached for on problems whose structure is nothing like an image or a sentence.
beats.fix: Match the method to the structure of the data. Tabular columns are heterogeneous, individually meaningful and often uninformative, which suits models that select among features rather than compose them.
beats.cost: The conclusion is empirical and bounded by the regime it was measured in, so it holds for datasets of the size and shape that were benchmarked rather than as a universal rule.

interview.q: Why is the newer method not the default choice on tabular data?
interview.trap: Answering that there is not enough data, or that categorical features need better encoding. The benchmark specifically found the gap is not mostly due to categorical features and does not disappear after tuning — the explanation is inductive bias, not capacity or preprocessing.
